Although the reforms differ by jurisdiction, the direction has been remarkably consistent. Governments have tightened eligibility, increased impairment thresholds and narrowed the circumstances in which psychological injuries qualify for ongoing compensation. The objective has been clear: improve the long-term sustainability of workers’ compensation schemes that have come under increasing financial pressure. Whether those reforms ultimately achieve their intended objectives remains to be seen, but they raise an interesting question for the life insurance industry. items.excerpt: It’s only legal in one market. The life insurance market. That probably sounds ridiculous. After all, insider trading is one of the most serious offences in financial markets. If you buy or sell shares while possessing material information that the rest of the market doesn’t have, you can face enormous fines and years in prison. Why? Markets don’t run on money. They run on information. Prices are simply the market’s opinion of that information. When one participant possesses material information that the other side doesn’t, markets stop rewarding good decisions and start rewarding information asymmetry. Governments don’t simply discourage insider trading. They criminalise it. Because confidence in markets depends on participants competing on reasonably equal information. Now imagine a different market. The government launches a national lottery. Every ticket costs $10. Before buying your first ticket, only some people are offered a once-off $10 test. The test doesn’t tell you the winning numbers. Instead, it tells you things like: The winning numbers are all prime numbers. The number 3 appears three times. None of the numbers are greater than 25. You still don’t know the winning numbers. But every lottery ticket you buy for the rest of your life comes with information that nobody else has. Should you still pay the same $10 as everyone else? Most people would instinctively say no. Because you aren’t buying the same lottery ticket anymore. You’re buying it with information. Now think about a casino. Card counting isn’t illegal. If you have an exceptional memory, you’re free to do it. But casinos will politely escort you to the door the moment they realise you’re doing it. Why? Because information changes the odds. Exactly the sort of people who, not that long ago, might have seen actuarial science as an obvious career. I expected at least one of them to mention becoming an actuary. Not one did. That stayed with me. Around the same time, I read the now famous substack on the quiet decline of Australia’s life actuarial market. It articulated something many of us working in the industry have been feeling for years. The Australian life insurance industry isn’t just changing. I wonder whether it’s also quietly underinvesting in one of its most important long-term assets. Its future capability. An asset you won’t find on the balance sheet I’ve written previously about the idea of an Invisible Balance Sheet . Every company carefully manages the assets it can measure—capital, cash, technology and expenses. But every business also depends on assets that never appear in its financial statements. Trust. Institutional knowledge. Relationships. Culture. Leadership. And perhaps the most important of all... The next generation of talent. The life insurance industry spends a lot of time thinking about capital adequacy. I’m starting to wonder whether we should spend just as much time thinking about capability adequacy . Because capability compounds. Or disappears. The apprenticeship we never had to design For decades, the profession didn’t really have to think about how actuaries were developed. The system largely looked after itself. Universities produced graduates. Insurers and consultancies hired them. Graduates learned by doing. Reinsurers hired experienced actuaries.
